items.title: 22/7 is a very good approximation of pi for a reason
items.claim: The fraction 22/7 = 3.142857 is closer to pi than its small denominator suggests. The fractions 355/113 = 3.141593 are even closer — accurate to 6 decimal places with only 6-figure numbers.
items.prompt: Why are these particular fractions so good?

options.text: They are 'convergents' of pi's continued fraction expansion, which generates the BEST possible rational approximations — no smaller-denominator fraction can be closer
They are products of pi's digits
All irrationals have such good approximations

items.reveal_title: Continued fractions and best rational approximations
items.reveal:
Pi's continued fraction expansion begins: 3 + 1/(7 + 1/(15 + 1/(1 + 1/(292 + 1/(...))))). The 'convergents' formed by truncating give:
3/1, 22/7, 333/106, 355/113, 103993/33102, ...

Each convergent is the best rational approximation to pi for its denominator size (no fraction with a smaller or equal denominator is closer). This is a theorem of continued fractions.

The large coefficient 292 in pi's expansion is why 355/113 is so good — it means the next convergent, after 355/113, only kicks in at much larger denominators. So 355/113 is unusually accurate for its size.

The golden ratio phi has continued fraction 1 + 1/(1 + 1/(1 + ...)), all 1s — making it the irrational hardest to approximate by rationals. This 'most irrational' property is why phi appears in plant phyllotaxis and quasicrystals.

Diophantine approximation studies exactly how well an irrational can be approximated by rationals. Roth's theorem (1955) gives sharp bounds for algebraic numbers; the field overlaps with number theory at every turn.
items.why: Approximating irrationals feels like it should give roughly similar fractions. Continued fractions give a precise algorithm for the BEST approximations and reveal why some irrationals are 'harder' than others.

items.title: There are true statements about numbers that cannot be proved
items.claim: Hilbert (1900) hoped to put mathematics on a complete, consistent axiomatic foundation. In 1931, Kurt Gödel proved it impossible. Any system of axioms expressive enough to do basic arithmetic contains true statements that the system cannot prove.
items.prompt: What's the heart of Gödel's argument?

options.text: Gödel constructed a self-referential statement G: 'G cannot be proved within this system'. If the system could prove G, the system would prove something false (contradiction). If the system can't prove G, then G is true and unprovable

items.reveal:
Gödel encoded statements about mathematics AS numbers (Gödel numbering), so the system could 'talk about itself'. He then constructed a sentence asserting its own unprovability.

First incompleteness theorem: any consistent system strong enough to express arithmetic contains a true statement it cannot prove.
Second incompleteness theorem: such a system cannot prove its own consistency from within itself.

The results devastated Hilbert's program. They also bounded what computers can do: the halting problem (Turing 1936) is undecidable in essentially the same way.

Gödel was 25 when he proved it. Hilbert took it badly. Gödel later starved himself to death (1978) — convinced his food was being poisoned, he stopped eating when his wife was hospitalised.

Mathematics is still consistent (presumably), still useful, still extending — just provably incomplete.
items.why: Mathematics is treated as a closed, fully derivable system. Gödel showed any rich enough system has fundamental gaps — true things it can never prove.

items.title: 20% of people own 80% of the wealth — and 4% own 64%
items.claim: Vilfredo Pareto observed in 1896 that ~20% of Italians owned ~80% of the land. The pattern recurs in income, book sales, software bugs, city sizes, earthquake magnitudes. Apply 80/20 again to that 20%: 4% own 64%. And again: 0.8% own 51.2%.
items.prompt: Why is this 'fractal' inequality so common?

options.text: Many natural and social processes follow POWER LAWS: P(X > x) is proportional to x to some negative power. Power-law distributions exhibit self-similarity at all scales, including the recursive 80/20 split
It is true only for exactly 20%

items.reveal:
A power-law distribution: the probability that a quantity exceeds x is proportional to x^(-alpha), for some exponent alpha. The Pareto distribution is the canonical example.

When alpha is in a particular range (specifically when the exponent gives an 80/20 split), the distribution is 'self-similar': the top 20% has 80% of the total; within that top 20%, the top 20% (i.e., the top 4%) holds 80% of THEIR share (i.e., 64% of the whole).

Key examples:
- US household wealth: top 20% own ~85%; top 1% own ~32%.
- Earthquakes: each unit increase in magnitude is ~10x less frequent.
- City sizes (Zipf's law, also power law).
- Web site visits, book sales, file sizes, software bug counts.
- Word frequencies in language (Zipf).

Generative mechanisms: 'rich-get-richer' (preferential attachment, scale-free networks — Barabási, Albert 1999); multiplicative growth; minimax processes.

Power laws contrast with normal distributions (bell curves) where extreme values are vanishingly rare. In power-law distributions, extreme values dominate — and you can't reason about averages as 'typical'.
items.why: Equality intuitions assume bell curves. Many real distributions are power laws — where the top few items dwarf the rest, and inequality is built into the math.
